lead: In a two-phase region steam is part liquid and part vapour. Its properties are not ideal-gas values. Steam tables list saturated liquid and saturated vapour; a single number, quality, fixes the mixture. The same idea powers the steam plant and the refrigerator: you read two properties, locate the state, and calculate the rest.
prereq: You need Unit 1 enthalpy, Unit 2 phase diagrams and latent heat, and Unit 3 steam cycles.

blocks.text: At a given pressure, water boils at one temperature, the saturation temperature Tsat. The liquid just before boiling is saturated liquid. Its properties carry subscript f: vf [m³/kg], hf [kJ/kg], sf [kJ/(kg·K)]. The vapour just after boiling is saturated vapour, subscript g. Between them is a wet mixture.

Quality x is the mass fraction of vapour: x = m<sub>g</sub>/(m<sub>f</sub> + m<sub>g</sub>). m<sub>f</sub> is mass of saturated liquid [kg]; m<sub>g</sub> is mass of saturated vapour [kg]. x = 0 is saturated liquid, x = 1 is saturated vapour, 0 < x < 1 is wet mixture.
M = (1 − x)M<sub>f</sub> + xM<sub>g</sub> = M<sub>f</sub> + x(M<sub>g</sub> − M<sub>f</sub>)
blocks.where: M stands for v, u, h or s per kg; M<sub>f</sub> is the saturated-liquid value; M<sub>g</sub> is the saturated-vapour value; x is quality.

blocks.text: h = h<sub>f</sub> + x h<sub>fg</sub>,  v = v<sub>f</sub> + x(v<sub>g</sub> − v<sub>f</sub>)
blocks.where: h<sub>fg</sub> = h<sub>g</sub> − h<sub>f</sub> is latent heat of vaporisation [kJ/kg]; v<sub>g</sub> − v<sub>f</sub> is the volume change on vaporisation [m³/kg]. Use h<sub>fg</sub>, never h<sub>g</sub>, in the second term.

blocks.text: Above the saturation temperature at the same pressure the vapour is superheated. Read its properties from the superheated table, not from the saturated columns. The degree of superheat is T − Tsat [K or °C].

sections.h3: Reading a steam table and interpolating

items: Compare the given T with T<sub>sat</sub> at the given P, or the given P with P<sub>sat</sub> at the given T. This tells you liquid, wet mixture or superheated vapour.
For a wet mixture, use one known property to find x. For example x = (h − h<sub>f</sub>)/h<sub>fg</sub> or x = (v − v<sub>f</sub>)/(v<sub>g</sub> − v<sub>f</sub>).
Use x in M = M<sub>f</sub> + x(M<sub>g</sub> − M<sub>f</sub>) for every other property. Do not use x for temperature or pressure; both stay at saturation.
For superheated vapour, enter the superheated table at the given P and T. If the table has no exact T or P, interpolate.

blocks.where: z is the known value (T, P or h); y is the wanted property; (z₁, y₁) and (z₂, y₂) are the two table points that bracket z. Keep x for quality only, never for the interpolation variable.

blocks.text: Interpolate only between two rows of the same table region. Interpolating between saturated liquid and saturated vapour rows with T or P gives nonsense, because both rows share the same T and P.

sections.h3: Diagrams: P-v, T-s, h-s and P-h

blocks.text: A property diagram plots two properties so a cycle becomes a path. The saturation dome is the two-phase region. Under the dome, an isobar is also an isotherm: at fixed P, T stays at T<sub>sat</sub> until the last liquid evaporates. That horizontal line is the easiest feature to spot.

On a T-s diagram the area under a reversible path is heat. On an h-s diagram, the Mollier chart, a vertical drop is an isentropic turbine or nozzle, so it is used for steam turbines. On a P-h diagram, an isenthalpic throttle is a vertical line, so it is used for refrigeration and heat pumps.

Quality lines run across the dome. The critical point closes the dome; above it there is no liquid-vapour split. Some syllabi call these thermodynamic property charts. Use them for quick reads and for checking table values, not as a replacement for the table when an exact number is needed.

figure.caption: The line runs from saturated liquid to saturated vapour at 10 bar; the marked point is the worked example at x = 0.90.

spec.aria: A straight line of enthalpy against quality at 10 bar, from 762.8 to 2778.1 kJ/kg, with a marked point at quality 0.90 and enthalpy 2576.6 kJ/kg.

examples.question: Steam at 10 bar has quality 0.90. Given h<sub>f</sub> = 762.8 kJ/kg, h<sub>fg</sub> = 2015.3 kJ/kg, v<sub>f</sub> = 0.001127 m³/kg and v<sub>g</sub> = 0.1944 m³/kg, calculate the specific enthalpy h and specific volume v of the mixture.
steps: The state is a wet mixture because 0 < x < 1. Use the saturated-liquid and saturated-vapour values at 10 bar.
Write the enthalpy formula: h = h<sub>f</sub> + x h<sub>fg</sub>.
Write the volume formula: v = v<sub>f</sub> + x(v<sub>g</sub> − v<sub>f</sub>).
Compute the volume change: v<sub>g</sub> − v<sub>f</sub> = 0.1944 − 0.001127 = 0.193273 m³/kg.
examples.check:
hf = 762.8
hfg = 2015.3
x = 0.90
vf = 0.001127
vg = 0.1944
h = hf + x * hfg
v = vf + x * (vg - vf)
print(round(h, 1))
print(round(v, 4))

traps: Taking h = h<sub>g</sub> for a wet mixture: at 10 bar and x = 0.90 this gives 2778.1 kJ/kg, about 201 kJ/kg too high.

Substituting h<sub>g</sub> in place of h<sub>fg</sub>: h = h<sub>f</sub> + x h<sub>g</sub> = 762.8 + 0.90 × 2778.1 = 3263.1 kJ/kg, about 686 kJ/kg too high, because x h<sub>f</sub> is then counted an extra time.
Treating quality as a volume fraction. Quality is a mass fraction; volume is then found from v = v<sub>f</sub> + x(v<sub>g</sub> − v<sub>f</sub>).
Interpolating in the wrong region: saturated tables for superheated steam, or superheated tables inside the dome.
Forgetting that T and P are not averaged with quality in the wet region: both stay at T<sub>sat</sub> and P<sub>sat</sub>.
Mixing units: v is in m³/kg, h in kJ/kg, and h<sub>fg</sub> is already per kg. Do not multiply h<sub>fg</sub> by total mass unless you want total enthalpy.

quiz.q: Define quality x for a wet mixture and state its range.
quiz.a: x = m<sub>g</sub>/(m<sub>f</sub> + m<sub>g</sub>), where m<sub>g</sub> is mass of saturated vapour and m<sub>f</sub> is mass of saturated liquid. The range is 0 ≤ x ≤ 1.

quiz.q: Why does h = h<sub>f</sub> + x h<sub>fg</sub> use h<sub>fg</sub> and not h<sub>g</sub>?
quiz.a: h<sub>f</sub> already includes the liquid enthalpy. The extra enthalpy for vapour is the latent heat h<sub>fg</sub> = h<sub>g</sub> − h<sub>f</sub>. Writing h = h<sub>f</sub> + x h<sub>g</sub> adds h<sub>f</sub> once directly and x h<sub>f</sub> again inside x h<sub>g</sub>, so the result is too high by x h<sub>f</sub>.

quiz.q: At 10 bar, h<sub>f</sub> = 762.8 kJ/kg and h<sub>fg</sub> = 2015.3 kJ/kg. Find h for x = 0.80.
At 10 bar, v<sub>f</sub> = 0.001127 m³/kg and v<sub>g</sub> = 0.1944 m³/kg. Find v for x = 0.50.
A student uses h<sub>g</sub> = 2778.1 kJ/kg as the enthalpy of steam at 10 bar with x = 0.90. What is wrong, and how large is the error?
quiz.a: h<sub>g</sub> is saturated vapour at x = 1. For x = 0.90 the correct value is h = 762.8 + 0.90 × 2015.3 = 2576.6 kJ/kg. The student's value is 2778.1 − 2576.6 = 201.5 kJ/kg too high.

quiz.q: Why is an isobar horizontal in the wet region of a P-v or T-s diagram?
quiz.a: At a fixed pressure, a pure substance changes phase at a single saturation temperature. While liquid and vapour coexist, T remains at T<sub>sat</sub> and P remains fixed, so the path is horizontal on those axes.

quiz.q: Which property diagram is most convenient for a refrigeration throttle, and why?
quiz.a: A P-h diagram. A throttle is isenthalpic, so it is a vertical line on P-h; the evaporator and condenser are horizontal lines where pressure is constant. Enthalpy values are read directly.

beyond: Not for the exam. Digital steam tables use the IAPWS-IF97 formulation, an international standard that reproduces printed steam-table values without interpolation. Plant operators and turbine designers link these tables to plant data historians, so a measured pressure and temperature become enthalpy and entropy in real time. Refrigeration engineers use P-h charts in the same way for quick cycle checks. Search for IAPWS-IF97 steam properties, Mollier chart, and P-h diagram refrigeration cycle.
